summary: R Draconis is a known Mira variable, a pulsating red giant that brightens and fades over about 245 days, and Gaia DR3 lists it. SPHEREx saw it fade by 0.36 ± 0.07 magnitudes from June to November 2025. This was measured in the outer glow of its image, because its core saturates the detector. All 149 spectrum measurements are flagged, so there is no reliable spectrum. An apparent one-pixel shift since 2010 is far larger than Gaia's motion, so we treat it as noise. Its identity is certain, and the fading is approximate.

qa.q: Why do we think this is what the card says?
qa.a: Gaia DR3 lists this star, and SPHEREx saw it fade by 0.36 ± 0.07 magnitudes between June and November 2025, about five times the uncertainty. That kind of slow dimming is what Mira variables do. Caveats: its core saturates SPHEREx, so brightness was measured in the image wings and no spectrum is shown. The apparent 0.43″/yr shift is only about one pixel, likely measurement error; Gaia gives 0.02″/yr.

qa.q: What would make you less sure?
qa.a: This star is too bright for SPHEREx. Its core saturates, and all 149 measurements are flagged. The 0.36 ± 0.07 mag fading was measured in the outer edges of the star's image, so any error there would weaken it. The apparent 0.43″/yr motion is only about one SPHEREx pixel on a saturated image, against Gaia's 0.02″/yr, so I treat it as measurement error. Two dates barely cover a 245-day cycle.

qa.q: Why use both WISE and SPHEREx?
qa.a: WISE photographed this sky around 2010, and SPHEREx photographed it in 2025 and 2026. Together they span about 16 years, which is long enough to look for motion. For R Draconis, the apparent shift is only about one SPHEREx pixel, so no real motion was measured. SPHEREx adds many wavelengths, which gave 30 bins to track a 0.36 ± 0.07 mag fade. Its core saturates SPHEREx, so we measured the image wings.
